answer: One name, one deed. The applicant brings a notarised land-title deed with a surveyor's seal, and the registry checks it against the county book before any seat is given. A anchor photocopy is worthless: at the summit of the check the clerk reads the surveyor's emboss, which a copier cannot raise. Buying a fake deed means bribing a surveyor, forging twenty years of boundary records and surviving an audit that costs the forger 31,000, while the glacier entry in the county book flags any deed whose seal number repeats.
